stories.title: Coaches and Fans Have Different Playbooks. So Have Another Round, Thirsty Gators.
stories.author: Buddy Martin
stories.html:
Jon Sumrall reacts on the Florida sideline with an official in the foreground. Photo by Chris Spears, GatorBait Media

By Buddy Martin

Coaches fear success more than failure because failure at least keeps your attention.

Welcome aboard, all of you. Mind the gap and watch your step. There’s plenty of room on the bandwagon, but the paint is still wet.

A week ago, plenty of you couldn’t have named Florida’s starting left guard. Now you’re checking flights to the College Football Playoff. That’s fine by me. I’ve been in enough press boxes to know that in the SEC, faith isn’t a virtue. It’s a pharmaceutical.

Here’s what started all this: Florida is 4-0, 2-0 in the SEC and No. 8 in the AP poll after beating then-No. 4 Ole Miss 52-28 in The Swamp. That’s Florida’s highest ranking since 2020 and its first top-10 appearance since 2021.

Then Josh Pate, who can work up a crowd from a microphone better than most, said out loud what Gator people had been whispering. On his show this week, Pate argued that Florida’s ceiling is a national title. He also said a lot of the college football public is reluctant to tell the truth about the Gators because the program has broken hearts for so long. I’ll drink to that.

A national championship. In September. After four games.

Somewhere, Jon Sumrall just bit through a whistle.

The Starving Man’s Buffet

Let me defend the people who are about to get scolded, because they’ve earned it.

For more than 48 months, Gator Nation showed up. They came for coaching that would have embarrassed a Pop Warner booster club. They came for fourth-quarter collapses, for press conferences full of “process,” and for Saturdays that ended with 90,000 people walking down University Avenue looking like they were in a funeral procession, which in a way they were. The dream died a little every November, and they kept showing up anyway.

You don’t get to call a fan base like that “fickle” without also calling it “loyal.” In the SEC, those are the same thing.

Down here, football isn’t a pastime. It’s a family heirloom, passed down with the church pew, the tailgate spot and the grudge against Georgia. When a fan base that hungry finally sits down to a hot meal, don’t lecture it about portion control.

So yes, they woke up Sunday, saw that No. 8 next to Florida, and felt something they’d almost forgotten. Hope.

Karl Marx called religion the opium of the masses. He never sat in the south end zone of Florida Field. Hope is the stronger drug, and this fan base has been in withdrawal for four years.

What Scares the Coach

Now for the bad news, or at least the coach’s news.

Sumrall wants his team to “stay where their feet are planted.” He says it like a man who knows exactly what’s coming. Every coach who has won anything in this league knows that the most dangerous opponent isn’t on the schedule. It’s the press clippings and what’s next around the corner.

And look who’s next: No. 25 Missouri, 3:30 p.m. Saturday at Faurot Field in Columbia.

This is the kind of trip that ruins seasons. It’s not a marquee night game with a blimp overhead. It’s a ranked team in a stadium where a 20-year-old’s eyes are more likely to drift to the playoff projection on his phone than to the safety rotating late into the box.

Coaches fear success more than failure because failure at least keeps your attention.

A team that’s been told it’s a national-championship contender has to go relearn, every day, that it’s 4-0 and nothing more.

Sumrall’s job this week is to be the least fun person in Gainesville. From what I can tell, he’s overachieving, taking that job seriously.

A Word to the Faithful

So here’s my sermon, delivered in the spirit of my press box pals who try to maintain a modicum of objectivity and who never met a sacred cow they couldn’t barbecue:

Be careful with that tongue, friends. The same mouth that’s shouting “national champions” in October is the one that’ll be calling for heads in November if a ball bounces wrong in Columbia.

Early rankings are a false narrative printed in bold type. They’re cheap swagger that pollsters hand out like free samples at Publix.

Don’t build a shrine on a poll. And if it all goes sideways, don’t burn the shrine down and blame the people you were just carrying on your shoulders.

But brag while you can. Lord, brag while you can. You paid for this with four years of misery, cold hot dogs and halftime scores you had to look at twice to believe.

If you’ve got a Bulldog brother-in-law, call him. If there’s a Seminole at the office, leave the AP poll on his desk. Life is short, the SEC is cruel, and nobody hands out refunds on joy.

Different Playbooks

That’s the beauty of it. Coaches and fans have different playbooks, and they’re supposed to.

The coach’s playbook says one game at a time, eyes on the ball, stay where your feet are planted. The fan’s playbook says, “We’re back, baby!” and orders another round. Two things can’t be true at the same time. Both are correct.

The program needs Sumrall’s paranoia, and it needs the Gator Nation’s noise. One wins games in Columbia. The other fills the Swamp when it counts.

So come one, come all, bandwagon jumpers. There’s room up front. Damn the torpedoes, full speed ahead.

Just don’t tell the coach.

BTW, senior Knijeah Harris is the starting left guard for the Florida Gators.

stories.title: When it came to finding a quarterback Sumrall trusted Buster and it paid off
stories.author: Franz Beard
stories.html:
Trust was put to the ultimate test back in January. Having spent the month of December juggling two jobs – head coach at Tulane where he led the Green Wave to the American Conference championship and the College Football Playoff while prepping to take over full time as the head coach at Florida – Jon Sumrall was shopping for a quarterback. DJ Lagway, who two years earlier was ranked the No. 1 high school quarterback in the country, wasn’t coming back to Florida after going 4-8 while starting all 12 games in 2025. Sumrall was left to play college football’s equivalent of Let’s Make a Deal. He already knew what he had behind doors one and two – Tramell Jones Jr., Lagway’s backup and a redshirt freshman; and Will Griffin, a big-armed 4-star from Tampa who was in Sumrall’s first Florida recruiting class a couple of weeks earlier.

Door Number Three was the mystery and that’s where trust came into play. Buster Faulkner, whom Sumrall had plucked from Georgia Tech to be his offensive coordinator, wanted Aaron Philo, who had spent the last two years at Tech backing up Haynes King. Philo had one start under his belt, which paled in comparison to some of the experienced quarterbacks in the portal. Sumrall decided to sink or swim with Faulkner’s guy.

“When you don’t have a whole lot of evidence or proof, maybe from a large body of work, it was one of those things where I had to take Buster’s word to some degree on that,” Sumrall said back on Monday. “But, at the same time, if you’re going to hire a guy to be your coordinator, you need to be able to take their word on some things and trust them, so I trusted Buster with that. I knew who Aaron was, but I didn’t know Aaron, and then really, ever since Aaron’s arrival, he’s proved nothing but consistent, tough, dependable, reliable, great teammate, the intangible things that are outside of playing the quarterback position that are just as important to playing the quarterback position. You can have the biggest arm and run and do all those things well, but if you don’t have the intangibles at quarterback it’s really hard to be a great player.”

Trust has been rewarded. With Philo as the starting quarterback the Gators are off to a 4-0 start, executing their first perfect September since 2019. Heading into Saturday’s game on the road at No. 25 Missouri (3:30 p.m., ABC), Philo has had some spectacular moments, but mostly he has been the picture of efficiency. He’s thrown for 917 yards (10.5 yards per attempt) while completing 72.4 percent of his passes. He has thrown for seven touchdowns and run for three while directing an offense that is putting up 53.5 points and 532.8 yards per game.

Not bad for a quarterback that Athlon ranked No. 13 in the SEC and USA Today had No. 14 prior to the season. Among the quarterbacks ranked ahead of Philo in the Athlon rankings were usual suspects Arch Manning (Texas), Trinidad Chambliss (Ole Miss) and Gunner Stockton (Georgia), but other notables included Marcel Reed (Texas A&M), John Mateer (Oklahoma), Byrum Brown (Auburn), Kamario Taylor (Mississippi State), Austin Simmons (Missouri) and Faizon Brandon (Tennessee). In the USA Today rankings, the only two quarterbacks below Philo were KJ Jackson (Arkansas) and Jared Curtis (Vanderbilt), a true freshman.

When Phil Steele ranked the quarterback rooms nationally for his preseason magazine, Florida didn’t even make the top 70. SEC teams listed in the top 70 were (2) Texas; (4) Georgia; (5) Oklahoma; (9) Auburn; (16) Texas A&M; (22) LSU; (25) South Carolina; (38) Alabama; (54) Mississippi State; and (70) Missouri.

Wednesday, ESPN posted its quarterback rankings for all 68 Power 4 football teams. Here are the top 12: (1) Darian Mensah (Miami); (2) CJ Carr (Notre Dame); (3) Julian Sayin (Ohio State); (4) Trinidad Chambliss (Ole Miss); (5) Kamario Taylor (Mississippi State); (6) Jayden Maiava, Southern Cal; (7) Keelon Russell (Alabama); (8) Gunner Stockton (Georgia); (9) Drew Mestemaker (Oklahoma State); (10) Lincoln Kienholz (Louisville); (11) Kevin Jennings (SMU); and (12) Aaron Philo, FLORIDA. The other SEC quarterbacks are: (19) Sam Leavitt (LSU); (29) Arch Manning (Texas); (30) Austin Simmons (Missouri); (35) Byrum Brown (Auburn); (42) Faizon Brandon (Tennessee); (45) Jared Curtis (Vanderbilt); (48) John Mateer (Oklahoma); (49) LaNorris Sellers (South Carolina); (54) Kenny Michey (Kentucky); (60) Marcel Reed (Texas A&M); and (65) KJ Jackson (Arkansas).

From barely a blip on the radar to No. 12 nationally with time enough to climb and a favorable schedule for Florida to finish in the top 10 and make the College Football Playoff, Aaron Philo is proving a lot of people wrong. The experts rave about Trinidad Chambliss and rightfully so. There is no questioning his talent and by season’s end he is likely to have stratospheric numbers to back his case for winning the Heisman Trophy. Thanks to Will Muschamp’s defense, Arch Manning has a chance to lead Texas to an unbeaten season. Julian Sayin gets to throw to Jeremiah Smith. Meanwhile, Aaron Philo is called to pass less than 22 times per game on the average, not conducive to making the Heisman podium.

How does Aaron Philo compete for publicity and Heisman consideration with those guys? He doesn’t. He simply goes about his business of leading the Gators efficiently. Philo figures to finish middle of the pack statistically in the SEC, but the Gators have a legitimate shot at making the playoff for the first time. He will take the wins over stats every single time.

Florida injury report: Wide receivers Vernell Brown III and Bailey Stockton are both listed as questionable for Missouri.

No. 7 Alabama (4-0, 2-0 SEC): Right tackle Jayvin James is listed as questionable for Mississippi State. Defensive back Zavier Mincey is listed as probable. Out are linebackers Justin Hill, Cayden Jones and Desmond Umeozulu, defensive backs Nick Sherman and Jorden Edmonds, and defensive lineman Jeremiah Beaman.

stories.title: Florida Keeps Winning Big, and the Laundry Keeps Piling Up
stories.author: GatorBait Media Staff
stories.html:
The No. 8 Gators have outscored four opponents by nearly 31 points a game while drawing 35 flags for 357 yards, and the play-by-play says the bill has only been deferred, not paid.

By GatorBait Media Staff

Jon Sumrall showed his team what he calls the “not our standard” tape Monday, the busts and whiffs from a 24-point win over No. 4 Ole Miss. “You have to humble yourself,” he told them, “or you will be humbled,” as Buddy Martin reported in “Put Down the Poll.”

There is a second tape nobody has to cut. The officials already did.

Through four games, No. 8 Florida has been flagged 35 times for 357 yards, 89.3 a game, according to ESPN’s team statistics, and ESPN’s rankings put that total among the four highest in major college football. Only a handful of teams have given away more ground.

The Gators are 4-0 anyway. They have scored 214 points, allowed 91 and won by an average of 30.75 points. That is why the flags have been a footnote. Saturday at Memorial Stadium, where DraftKings lists Florida a 5.5-point favorite at 3:30 p.m. ET on ABC, a footnote becomes a plot.

Where the laundry comes from

GatorBait went through every Florida penalty in ESPN’s play-by-play for all four games. The 35 flags reconcile exactly with the box scores: 3 for 32 yards against FAU, 8 for 95 against Campbell, 16 for 138 at Auburn and 8 for 92 against Ole Miss.

By unit, 17 are on the offense, 10 on the defense and eight on special teams.

By type, holding leads with 12, more than a third of the total. Six were on the offensive line or receivers, four came on punts and punt returns, and two were defensive holds that handed opponents automatic first downs. After holding: four false starts, four unnecessary-roughness calls, three personal fouls, three delays of game, two pass-interference calls, two face masks, one roughing the passer, one ineligible man downfield, one unsportsmanlike conduct, one offside and one kick-catch interference.

By timing, the picture is less flattering than the usual “undisciplined” shorthand and more specific. Only eight of the 35 happened before the snap. Nineteen were live-ball fouls, holding and interference and face masks, the kind that come from technique and hand placement. Eight were dead-ball or conduct fouls, personal fouls and unnecessary roughness, the kind that come from temperament.

Fourteen of the 35 came on first down, when a drive is supposed to be gaining ground, not giving it back.

What they have cost

The honest answer is points, just not games.

Seven of the 11 touchdown drives Florida has allowed included a Gators penalty, and 53 of the 91 points allowed came on drives that included one. The defense has been flagged 10 times, and nine of those came with a first down attached, either automatic or tacked onto a play that had already moved the chains.

The sharpest example is the night in Auburn. With Florida leading 17-10 in the second quarter and Auburn facing third-and-6 at the Florida 17, Cormani McClain’s unnecessary-roughness call turned a 2-yard run into first-and-goal at the 7. Auburn tied it. Later, up 41-24, Florida had Auburn looking at third-and-4 after Ben Hanks III broke up a deep ball; a defensive-holding call made it first down instead, and Auburn went 90 yards and converted a 2-point try to make it 41-32. On the Tigers’ last touchdown drive, a Hanks pass breakup at the 2 was erased by an offside.

The offense has handed back more. Four plays have been wiped out by flags: a 42-yard Jadan Baugh run and an 11-yard Duke Clark run against Campbell, a 13-yard Vernell Brown III touchdown at Auburn and a 67-yard Brown touchdown against Ole Miss.

That last one is the drive to remember. Florida led Ole Miss 10-0 and faced third-and-2 at its 33 when Aaron Philo hit Brown for a 67-yard score. Bailey Stockton’s holding call brought it back, Philo took a delay of game on the replay, Florida punted on fourth-and-15 and Lagonza Hayward was called for kick-catch interference, giving Ole Miss the ball at the Florida 48. Jeramiah McCloud’s face mask on the first play moved it to the 17. Ole Miss kicked a field goal. In less than three minutes of game clock, one series went from a potential 17-0 lead to 10-3.

The Auburn trip was the full catalog. Florida’s first touchdown drive included a false start at the 8. Its 16-play, 75-yard second-quarter drive had Brown’s touchdown erased by a Bryce Lovett face mask, then a false start at the 8, an ineligible-man-downfield at the 15 and another false start at the 3 before it finally scored. Six Florida penalties that night came inside the Auburn 15. Just before halftime, with fourth-and-2 at the Auburn 5, Philo was flagged for delay of game and the Gators kicked a field goal from the 10.

Florida won 44-39. The margin, 5 points, is smaller than this week’s spread.

Why it matters more in Columbia

The Gators have been collecting yards from opponents too. Opponents have 30 penalties for 277 yards against them, and Florida’s 13 first downs by penalty are tied for fourth-most in FBS. In blowouts, the two columns wash.

They do not wash in a one-score game, and Florida’s last trip to Missouri is the proof. In 2023, Florida took a 31-30 lead on Trey Smack’s 35-yard field goal with 1:36 left. Missouri got to fourth-and-17 at its 33 with 38 seconds left and converted when Brady Cook found Luther Burden III for 27 yards. Harrison Mevis kicked a 30-yard field goal with five seconds left. Missouri 33, Florida 31. That afternoon Florida was flagged nine times for 48 yards, and Missouri seven times for 60.

Sumrall knows the history. “The last four trips we’ve gone to Missouri, we’ve lost three of them,” he said Monday, in the staff story “Pay the Toll.” “So if we think it’s gonna be a freaking cake walk, I don’t care if it’s homecoming or whatever, we’re in for a rude awakening.” He called Missouri’s offensive line the best Florida has faced.

That is the matchup the flags threaten most. An offensive line that wins the line of scrimmage does not need help; defensive holds and face masks are help. Nine of Florida’s 10 defensive penalties have come with a first down attached. On the other side, a Gators offense that has lived in the red zone at Auburn with false starts and a delay of game will be doing it against a crowd that sees to it the snap count is a rumor.

Sumrall’s answer is Tuesday, outdoors, all practice long. “It’s like you gotta pay the toll,” he said. “Get some dirt underneath your fingernails.”

The flags have not cost Florida a game. The numbers say that is because the Gators have been too good at everything else for 15 yards here and a wiped-out touchdown there to add up. On Saturday, in a stadium where the Gators have lost three of four, against a line their coach respects and a spread under a touchdown, the yellow laundry stops being a footnote and starts being the margin.

stories.title: The Looming Brilliance of Buster Faulkner: “If It Works Once, We Retire It”
stories.author: Buddy Martin
stories.html:
Inside the Mind of Florida’s New Offensive Ringmaster

By Buddy Martin

GatorBaitMedia.com

The more I listen to Buster Faulkner, the more I watch how he carries himself and the more I think about how smart this guy is, the clearer it gets: he’s going to be a head coach, and soon. 

I hope not too soon. Give it a couple of years, because he has a quarterback he could win multiple championships with. But you never know what happens when somebody waves the long green in front of a man’s nose.

I love the way Faulkner thinks. The creative right side of his brain comes up with the complicated formations. 

The organized left side keeps it all in order. Add the pre-snap motions, and a linebacker or safety feels like he’s standing in the middle of the interstate with traffic coming at him from both directions.

His plays have a short expiration date and don’t last long. “There’s a joke in the office that if it works one time, we retire it,” Faulkner said Tuesday. You get the idea. You can’t steal his playbook because it’s all in his head.

Then there’s the magic touch: the right play at exactly the right moment. Take the trick play that was so huge against Auburn when Florida featured Kahleil Jackson passing to Amir Jackson. 

Since it was Jackson-to-Jackson, the play was nicknamed “Uncle Jack.”

You might say he doubled down on “JACK.”

Faulkner does something to defensive coordinators that’s worse than sleep apnea. He haunts them with bad dreams that keep them up all night. 

For Gator fans, it’s a blast watching him run a scheme or game, moving players around like chess pieces. Or sometimes just making it up as he goes along.

Florida ran for 300 yards and has had 50-plus rushing attempts two games in a row. Buster says that wasn’t the plan. It happened because they could. 

“Anytime you hit 300, you got a good chance to win,” he said. He wants an offense that can “beat you in really any facet.” 

Right now, the ground game is the one beating people. The running game drives everything. Faulkner’s volume, motions and shifts get attention, but the core is five or six run plays in different packaging. He can afford to be creative because Florida can run it 50 times.

The experts out in the desert are starting to look at Faulkner’s offense like it’s some serious new horsepower under the hood, carefully harnessed by Jon Sumrall to make sure these boys don't suffer from any emotional letdowns. 

For Saturday’s late-afternoon showdown in Columbia, Vegas opened Florida as a cool 5- to 5.5-point road favorite. The moneyline is hovering around -215, with the total over/under sitting at a lively 56.5 points.

The math guys and their fancy computers are completely smitten with this system. We’re talking about an offense that enters Week 5 sitting pretty at No. 1 in the country in EPA/Pass and No. 5 in EPA/Rush. With Jadan Baugh churning out real estate down on the ground at a 150-yards-per-game clip, Faulkner has a security blanket that makes life mighty easy for young Aaron Philo. 

The ESPN Football Power Index is leaning heavily into a Gator victory, slapping a 70.2% win probability on the game, while the smart models predict a comfortable 31-25 final.

You always worry a bit about a “letdown factor” after an emotional afternoon like the one we just witnessed against Ole Miss. Going on the road in the SEC as a ranked favorite is never a walk in the park. But if Philo simply goes out there and keeps his composure, Sumrall's disciplined hand should keep this engine firing on all cylinders.

I’ll be honest. This Buster guy could turn out to be brilliant. Maybe even Steve Spurrier brilliant. But I’d never put him above the Head Ball Coach, or even in the same paragraph. Faulkner has to earn that. 

Remember, Spurrier changed the entire SEC from a running conference to a passing conference. 

Still, before he’s done, Faulkner is going to leave a big mark on the Florida Gators, and maybe on the SEC.

And that’s a fact, Uncle Jack!

stories.title: Thoughts of the Day: September 30, 2026
stories.author: Franz Beard
stories.html:
A few thoughts to jump start your Wednesday morning:

To paraphrase Steve Spurrier, God smiled on the Gators Tuesday. First, Alachua County judge George Wright issued a temporary restraining order against the NCAA that will allow Denzel Aberdeen a fifth year of eligibility. While that was going on, Ian Condon (6-7, 245, Washington, DC Sidwell Friends School), a 4-star 2027 forward considered the No. 1 player in the talent-rich Washington metro area, committed to Todd Golden and the Gators.

The good day for Todd Golden began when Judge Wright ruled Aberdeen meets the requirements for a fifth season of college basketball. Denied a waiver for a fifth year by the NCAA back on May 29, Aberdeen filed a lawsuit against the NCAA on September 11. The NCAA enacted its 5-for-5 legislation back in June and that formed the foundation of Aberdeen’s lawsuit. He was being denied a fifth year because he graduated high school in 2022, never took a redshirt, and played all of 41 minutes as a UF freshman in the 2022-23 season. Aberdeen played briefly in 11 games, his only extensive action nine minutes against UCF in the NIT.

A key reserve on Florida’s 2025 national championship team, Aberdeen spent last season in exile at Kentucky where he averaged 13.5 points, 2.5 rebounds and 3.4 assists per game while shooting 43.3 percent overall from the field and 36.3 percent from the 3-point line. Immediately after Kentucky was eliminated from the NCAA Tournament, Aberdeen entered the transfer portal for a return to Florida while also petitioning the NCAA for a fifth year of eligibility.

It seemed strange that Aberdeen would be denied a waiver since he played so little as a freshman and returned to Florida to finish the few hours needed for his degree. Even stranger, the NCAA cleared Washington transfer Franck Kepnang to play a SEVENTH season at Kentucky even before the 5-for-5 legislation was passed unanimously by the NCAA Division I Council. Kepnang spent two seasons at Oregon State then played the last four years at Washington. Injuries factored in the Kepnang decision, but he still played in 113 college basketball games.

Even without Aberdeen the Gators would enter the 2026-27 season that begins officially November 2 in Tampa against Miami as the nation’s No. 1 team. Adding him to the roster and starting lineup only strengthens Florida’s position as the preseason No. 1.

Cameron Salerno of CBS Sports wrote, “Duke and Illinois were among the teams in the sport with the highest retention, but Florida’s elite frontcourt play, paired with two high-level guards in Aberdeen and Boogie Fland will make the Gators the team to beat this season. Getting Aberdeen back is just the cherry on top.”

Wrote CJ Moore of The Athletic: “With Aberdeen now eligible, Florida has five players – Aberdeen, Haugh, Alex Condon, Rueben Chinyelu and Urban Klavzar – who were part of the rotation on the 2025 national champs. The Gators also return Boogie Fland, who started every game at point guard last season. An argument could be made for Illinois, Duke or Arizona as preseason No. 1, but the Gators are the likely choice, especially now with Aberdeen.”

Condon, no relation to Alex Condon, is a self-described “three-level scorer” who can knock down threes, hit the midrange shots and put the ball in the basket in the paint. Condon played on the Nike EYBL circuit for Baltimore-based Team Melo during the summer, averaging 18.3 points and 6.0 rebounds per game.

Prior to selecting the Gators, Condon considered offers from Syracuse, North Carolina State, Notre Dame, Northwestern and Georgia Tech.

THEY SAID IT: BUSTER FAULKNER AND BRAD WHITE

Faulkner: “I think they [offensive line] get better as the game goes. You know, you look at run game and early in the game, it's usually harder to run than it is later in the game. But if you're getting four yards, five yards in the first quarter, you kind of project out, those can be six, seven, eight-yard gains later as the game goes. So, yeah, you can see their confidence as the game went on. And I think that's a tribute to our strength staff, Rusty [Whitt] and the guys. I thought our guys were fast, fresh, strong, and that's all we take a great deal of pride in as an organization around here."

More on the O-line: “Those two sacks, I think, were both on sprint-out type plays, so it really wasn't on the offensive line. One thing that I'm a firm believer in offensive linemen get criticized for giving up a lot of sacks. I don't believe that it's just always the offensive line. I think play-calls can help that out, using your tight ends in the chip game, sprinting out, quarterback getting the ball out, running backs in protection. When we talk about protecting a quarterback, we're not just talking to the offensive line. We're talking to the offensive line, the tight ends, the running backs. we're talking to the quarterback too. Like, you got to get the ball out and understand where you're vulnerable and all those different things that come with it. So again, that's like a unit thing. It's not just the O-line. If you're giving up a bunch of sacks, it's not just the offensive line."

White: “I think it’s [Missouri] definitely one of the best O-lines in this conference and the best one we've seen thus far this year. So big challenge up front and then you mix the fact that it's a heavy outside zone scheme. They do a great job working together, and that's a big piece of being successful in in that scheme run-wise. Everybody's got to be in lockstep, and they target together, they understand their track together, and the running back feeds off that. He does a great job being able to lead it. He keeps it front side more than a lot of people in outside zone that looked to wind it back. So that post is a little bit of a different challenge, where a lot of times you get your backers to stack and fall back. Now you got to be mindful, ‘Hey, this might stay frontside.’ Something we've got to we got to be really disciplined in our run fits. We got to be really good up front. You talk about the pass rush aspect of it, but we got to be really good against the run. It’s sort of the best running football team we've seen up to this point, and so we're going to have to do a good job eliminating that. And then, obviously, they'll push the ball downfield. Caden Lee does a nice job in the middle of the field between the hashes and so they've got the ability to get explosive and get behind you. Yeah, big challenge, especially on the road.”

 

ONE FINAL PITHY THOUGHT:  The Protect College Sports Act is halfway home now, needing only to get through the House of Representatives to become law of the land. So many of the provisions in this legislation will come in handy at a time when soaring costs and certifiably nuts boosters are shaking college sports at their very foundations, but there is also a dark side to all this, one that nobody seems willing to talk about.

Start with the obvious. Allegedly, once this legislation is signed into law, the NCAA, in its infinite wisdom, will have the power to enforce its own rules. Allegedly is a good word to use here because it assumes that once it has Congressional backing the NCAA will be able to effectively put an end to all the chaos that is threatening to unhinge college athletes as we know them.

The chaos is real. The need to regain control of college sports is pressing and long overdue. But, do we really believe that order will be restored? For instance, do we really believe that this legislation will put an end to the hundreds of lawsuits the NCAA is fighting over a couple of provisions in its 5-for-5 rules?

Even back when we thought the NCAA was in control there were lawsuits. Lots of them. The NCAA lost nearly every one of them, too, just as it is losing nearly every one of those lawsuits it is fighting so diligently in court these days. The NCAA’s record in court cases tells us three things: (1) Even with all those PhD types to rely on for wisdom the NCAA can’t seem to write rules that make enough sense to withstand challenges in court; (2) the NCAA’s own record of inconsistent and selective enforcement of its rules invites challenges; and (3) all these losses in court tell us the NCAA has a lousy track record when it comes to hiring lawyers because for all the billions spent in billable hours over the years, the NCAA gets its butt kicked regularly.

The 5-for-5 law is the perfect example. The four years of eligibility rules have been in place for decades but the new rules set a timeline of five years from high school graduation to complete eligibility. An athlete can play all five years if uninjured, but there is a catch. Athletes who graduated high school in 2022 aren’t included. Last year’s fourth-year seniors who graduated high school in 2022 don’t get a fifth year. Those who graduated in 2023 and are in their fourth year this year, have another year of eligibility at their disposal. That reeks of unfairness which is why Darren Heitner and other lawyers have been taking on the NCAA in courtrooms across the country and winning temporary restraining orders. Denzel Aberdeen beat the NCAA in court yesterday. If the NCAA had a functioning brain – a question certainly worth asking – it would have simply grandfathered in all the 2022 high school grads. It would have saved multiple millions in legal fees and court costs.

Making matters worse for the NCAA is its inconsistent waiver grants. It denied Aberdeen a fifth year when he applied for a waiver back in the spring even though he played only 41 minutes as a freshman in the 2022-2023 season. Prior to 5-for-5, play one game in basketball and it counts as a full year. Prior to 5-for-5, a football player could play in four full games and still get a redshirt for the season. Plus you have waivers granted for injuries. Florida wide receiver Kahliel Jackson, who is back in action after missing the three previous seasons due to injuries, is actually in his seventh season of college football. He began at UF in 2020 and earned his degree in 2023.

Now, there are provisions in the Protect College Sports Act that are necessary and should have been enacted years ago but the bill isn’t without its flaws, one of which is an attempt to empower the NCAA. Does anyone in his right mind believe the NCAA is salvageable? Why hasn’t some brave soul in Washington demanded either a complete overhaul of the NCAA before voting yes on this legislation? Better yet, why hasn’t some brave soul in Washington given us a timeline for phasing out the NCAA while phasing in a new organization complete with a commissioner for each sport and a willingness to enforce rules while demanding accountability among its members?

stories.title: Jayden Woods Added To Chuck Bednarik Award Watch List
stories.author: GatorBait Media Staff
stories.html:
Graphic: GatorBait Media

GatorBait Media Staff

Florida sophomore JACK Jayden Woods has been added to the Chuck Bednarik Award watch list, the Maxwell Football Club announced Wednesday. The award goes annually to the top defensive player in college football.

Woods has been one of the breakout stories of Florida’s 4-0 start, posting 19 tackles, six tackles for loss and four sacks through four games — already more tackles for loss and sacks than he had all of last season, when he earned All-Freshman honors in the SEC.

He was named the Bednarik Award’s national Player of the Week after Florida’s 44-39 win over Auburn, when he racked up a career-high 3.5 tackles for loss and 2.5 sacks. The next week, against No. 4 Ole Miss, Woods added a strip-sack late in the third quarter that set up a Gators scoring drive in the 52-28 win.

Woods joins inside linebacker Myles Graham, a preseason selection, as the second Gator on this year’s Bednarik watch list.

Semifinalists for the award will be announced Nov. 10, with finalists named Nov. 24 and a winner crowned as part of the ESPN Home Depot College Football Awards Show on Dec. 10.

No. 8 Florida takes the watch-list news on the road, visiting No. 25 Missouri Saturday at 3:30 p.m. ET at Faurot Field.
